claims.text: The 1994 USAF report attributed the debris to Project Mogul Flight No. 4 and acknowledged the weather balloon explanation had been a cover story; 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' (24 June 1997) attributed body accounts to anthropomorphic parachute test dummies.
GAO/NSIAD-95-187 found that RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed and that no disposition authority for the destruction could be located.

claims.source: Inference from the 1994 USAF report and GAO/NSIAD-95-187
claims.text: The most durable fact about Roswell is administrative, not physical: the government has conceded in writing that it lied publicly about the recovery, and the unit's message traffic for the relevant period no longer exists. Reasoning: the 1994 report concedes the cover story; GAO documents the record destruction; the two facts together establish deliberate concealment independent of what the debris was.

desc: Roswell is a city in Chaves County in southeastern New Mexico, and in 1947 it was the home of Roswell Army Air Field and the 509th Bomb Group - at that moment the only atomic-capable bomb group in the world, the unit that had dropped the weapons on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. That single fact governs everything about the site's significance: whatever came down on the Foster Ranch, roughly seventy-five miles northwest near Corona in Lincoln County, came down inside the security envelope of the only nuclear strike force on Earth, and the recovery was executed by that force's own intelligence office. Rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris in late June 1947, reported it to Chaves County Sheriff George Wilcox on 6 July, and RAAF sent Maj. Jesse Marcel, the 509th's intelligence officer, and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps to retrieve it. On 8 July 1947 the base public information officer, 1st Lt. Walter Haut, issued a press release stating that 'the intelligence office of the 509th Bomb group of the Eighth Air Force, Roswell Army Air Field, was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc.' Within hours Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey, commanding Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth Army Air Field, retracted it in front of press photographers with weather officer Warrant Officer Irving Newton, presenting the material as a weather balloon and radar target. The Air Force's own two later reports - the 1994 report identifying the debris as Project Mogul Flight No. 4 balloon train material launched from Alamogordo, and 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' of 24 June 1997 attributing body reports to anthropomorphic parachute test dummies - concede the central structural point: the 1947 statement was a cover story, issued by the Army Air Forces, to protect a classified programme. What Roswell demonstrates for this board is therefore not settled by the debris identification. It is that the United States has admitted, in its own official reports, to fabricating a public explanation for a materiel recovery in 1947, and that when GAO audited the paper trail in 1995 it found that RAAF outgoing messages for October 1946 to December 1949 had been destroyed with no disposition authority located. The record of the recovery was removed. That is the fact that survives audit.
